crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Collecting Emissions Data
children.blurb: Collecting emissions data covers the activity data and contextual information needed to calculate greenhouse gas emissions across an organization's operations and value chain.

children.name: Checking Claims Against the Ledger
children.blurb: Checking claims against the ledger means comparing a sustainability or carbon claim with the accounting records that support it.

children.name: Combining Financial and Non-Financial Data
children.blurb: Combining financial and non-financial data in sustainability and carbon accounting means linking monetary figures from the general ledger, such as operating costs, capital expenditure, and revenue, with physical and social measures like greenhouse gas emissions, energy use, water withdrawal, and workforce metrics.

children.name: Drafting Sustainability Disclosures
children.blurb: Drafting sustainability disclosures covers the narrative and numerical parts of corporate reports on climate, emissions, workforce, community, governance, and supply chain matters.

children.name: Carbon Credit Records
children.blurb: Carbon credit records are the structured data that track the lifecycle of a carbon credit, from issuance through ownership changes to retirement.

sections.body: Sustainability and carbon accounting is the work of measuring, reporting, and verifying greenhouse gas emissions and related claims. AI is now used to pull emissions data from utility bills, meter readings, invoices, travel systems, and supplier surveys, then map that data to emission factors. It checks corporate claims against the underlying ledger, looking for gaps between what a company says and what its records show. It also helps combine financial and non financial data so that carbon costs, savings, and risks sit beside ordinary accounting lines. In disclosure drafting, AI produces first drafts of sustainability reports and regulatory filings from structured data and prior text. Carbon credit records are another target, where AI can track issuance, retirement, and registry entries across markets.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The field is partly solved at the level of document handling and data extraction. Parsing a PDF bill, reading a meter photo, or matching a supplier name to a database are tasks that modern systems do with reasonable reliability. What is not solved is scope 3 emissions, where data comes from many suppliers, in many formats, with different boundaries and estimates. Assurance is also unsolved, because an AI generated number is not an audited number, and auditors still need evidence, controls, and a clear trail. Carbon credit records remain difficult because registries differ, double counting is hard to detect, and quality claims are often unverifiable. The honest limit is that AI can accelerate accounting work, but it cannot make a weak dataset true or turn a draft into a verified disclosure.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages in this section form a chain from raw data to public statement. Collecting Emissions Data is the starting point, covering how source records are gathered, cleaned, and converted into usable totals. Checking Claims Against the Ledger then tests those totals against what a company has said publicly, which is where inconsistency and greenwashing risk surface. Combining Financial and Non Financial Data connects carbon figures to financial reporting, so a reader can see how emissions, costs, and assets interact. Drafting Sustainability Disclosures takes the combined record and turns it into narrative and tabular drafts for regulators and investors. Carbon Credit Records sits at the end of the chain, covering offsets, registries, retirement, and the accounting questions that surround them, while the site's 219 compliance and regulation pages give broader context for the rules that shape these tasks.
